title: EFFECTS OF INDOOR LIGHTING ON MOOD AND COGNITION
research_question: Do luminous settings act as mood inducers, and if so, do these mood valences impair or enhance ongoing cognitive processes?

participants.description: Aged 18-55, from Sweden. Experiment 1: 96 subjects, Experiment 2: 96 subjects.
participants.recruitment: local press and radio advertisements, paid 200 Swedish crowns (c. 30 U.S. dollars)

stimuli_or_exposures.description: A chamber-room (3.9 m × 3.8 m × 2.5 m) furnished as an office with neutral room-coloration (off-white walls/ceiling, off-white with grey floor patterns). Included a green flower, false windows with green curtains, green writing pads, and a PC. Heat and humidity were controlled. Lighting was provided by six ceiling-mounted fluorescent luminaires, each with four lamps. Two illuminance levels (300 lx vs 1500 lx) and two colour temperatures ('warm' white: 3000K/2950K vs 'cool' white: 4000K/4200K) were manipulated. Experiment 1 used high CRI (95), Experiment 2 used low CRI (51-58). Exposure time was approximately 85 minutes before the second mood measure, and 120 minutes total.

measures.instrument: Six general knowledge questions (recall) and 18 multiple-choice questions (recognition) based on a 7-page text about ancient culture (Carter, 1982)
Recall of three 16-word lists (positive, negative, neutral affective tones) presented on a PC screen

Evaluation sheet with 7-point scales on dimensions (qualifications, work-related skills, motivation, attitude, intelligence, concern, ability to get along, promotion, overall evaluation) for a fictitious employee (Baron et al., 1992)

measures.construct: Current affective state (positive and negative mood)
measures.instrument: PANAS (Positive Affect Negative Effect Scales) (Watson et al., 1988), 10 adjectives per dimension, 5-point scale
Seven 5-point unipolar items (glaring, dim, soft, bright, warm, intense, cool)

mechanisms: luminous milieu acting as a mood inducer, which in turn affects cognitive processes
mood-congruence hypothesis (memory performance related to mood valence)
halo effect (rater bias in performance appraisal)
moderators: Colour Rendering Index (CRI) (high vs low, between experiments)
implementation_implications: Criteria for good indoor lighting may need revision to account for females' and males' emotional and cognitive responses.

limitations: The performance appraisal task used only one gender for the ratee, limiting generalizability of halo effect findings.
Low CRI conditions (Experiment 2) may not have been distinct enough to produce gender differences in room light evaluations.
Low CRI conditions (Experiment 2) did not produce appropriate context cues for long-term recall and recognition, potentially explaining null recall results.
